title: Building Production Terraform Infrastructure Modules
description: A comprehensive Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC) course on designing reusable Terraform modules, GCS/S3 remote state locking, input validation, environment isolation, and automated CI/CD plan checks.
body: Master modular cloud infrastructure management. Learn how to structure DRY Terraform codebases, manage remote backend state locks in Google Cloud Storage, enforce input validation, isolate environments safely, and automate CI/CD plan checks with Atlantis or GitHub Actions.

sections.title: Section 1: DRY Modular Code Structure & State Management

lessons.title: Lesson 1.1: Structuring Reusable Terraform Modules
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Three Teams, Three Copy-Pasted VPCs

Your platform team started with one `main.tf` for the payments service's VPC. Six months later, three more teams copy-pasted that file for their own services. Now there are four slightly different VPC definitions, one of them missing the flow-log configuration security asked for, and nobody remembers which copy is 'the good one'. A single security fix now means four pull requests instead of one.

The fix is a **reusable module**: one source of truth for 'what a compliant VPC looks like', parameterized so each team supplies only what differs (project, region, CIDR range).

### Directory Layout

```text
infra/
├── modules/
│   ├── network/
│   │   ├── main.tf
│   │   ├── variables.tf
│   │   └── outputs.tf
│   └── cloud-run-service/
│       ├── main.tf
│       ├── variables.tf
│       └── outputs.tf
└── environments/
    ├── dev/
    │   ├── main.tf
    │   └── backend.tf
    ├── staging/
    │   ├── main.tf
    │   └── backend.tf
    └── prod/
        ├── main.tf
        └── backend.tf
```

`modules/` holds resource logic that never mentions an environment name. `environments/*/main.tf` only wires modules together with environment-specific inputs — this is what keeps drift out of the system.

### The Reusable Network Module

```hcl
# modules/network/variables.tf
variable "project_id" {
  type        = string
  description = "GCP project ID this VPC is created in"
}

variable "region" {
  type    = string
  default = "us-central1"
}

variable "subnet_cidr" {
  type        = string
  description = "CIDR range for the primary subnet, e.g. 10.10.0.0/20"
}

variable "enable_flow_logs" {
  type    = bool
  default = true
}

# modules/network/main.tf
resource "google_compute_network" "vpc" {
  project                 = var.project_id
  name                    = "vpc-${var.project_id}"
  auto_create_subnetworks = false
}

resource "google_compute_subnetwork" "primary" {
  project       = var.project_id
  name          = "subnet-${var.region}"
  ip_cidr_range = var.subnet_cidr
  region        = var.region
  network       = google_compute_network.vpc.id

  dynamic "log_config" {
    for_each = var.enable_flow_logs ? [1] : []
    content {
      aggregation_interval = "INTERVAL_5_SEC"
      flow_sampling        = 0.5
      metadata             = "INCLUDE_ALL_METADATA"
    }
  }
}

# modules/network/outputs.tf
output "network_id" {
  value = google_compute_network.vpc.id
}

output "subnet_id" {
  value = google_compute_subnetwork.primary.id
}
```

### Consuming the Module Per Environment

```hcl
# environments/prod/main.tf
module "network" {
  source           = "../../modules/network"
  project_id       = "acme-prod-472011"
  region           = "us-central1"
  subnet_cidr      = "10.20.0.0/20"
  enable_flow_logs = true
}

# environments/dev/main.tf
module "network" {
  source           = "../../modules/network"
  project_id       = "acme-dev-119832"
  region           = "us-central1"
  subnet_cidr      = "10.10.0.0/20"
  enable_flow_logs = false  # cheaper, faster iteration in dev
}
```

Every team now consumes the same `modules/network`. The security team's flow-log fix is one PR to `modules/network/main.tf` — every environment picks it up on its next `terraform apply`, instead of four separate hunts through copy-pasted files.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: A module boundary is a promise. Anything a caller can override should be a `variable`; anything the module owns internally (naming conventions, required labels) should NOT be exposed as a variable, or every caller will eventually drift anyway.

lessons.title: Lesson 1.2: Remote State Locking with GCS / S3 Backends
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: Two Engineers, One Corrupted State File

At 4:58pm on a Friday, two engineers both run `terraform apply` against the same production workspace within thirty seconds of each other. Both read the same state, both compute a plan, and both write back their own version of `terraform.tfstate`. Whichever `apply` finishes last silently overwrites the other's changes — Terraform's state file now disagrees with the real infrastructure it's supposed to represent, and the next `plan` shows dozens of unexpected diffs.

A **remote backend with locking** turns this race into a queue: the second `apply` blocks until the first one releases the lock, instead of corrupting shared state.

### GCS Backend Configuration (Native State Locking)

```hcl
# environments/prod/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "acme-prod-tfstate"
    prefix = "terraform/network"
  }
}
```

GCS backends use object generation preconditions for locking automatically — no extra resource required. Bootstrap the bucket itself (outside the module it protects, to avoid a chicken-and-egg problem):

```hcl
# bootstrap/main.tf — applied once, manually, before any other environment
resource "google_storage_bucket" "tfstate" {
  name                        = "acme-prod-tfstate"
  location                    = "US"
  force_destroy               = false
  uniform_bucket_level_access = true

  versioning {
    enabled = true  # every state write becomes a recoverable version
  }

  lifecycle_rule {
    condition { num_newer_versions = 20 }
    action    { type = "Delete" }
  }
}
```

### S3 + DynamoDB Backend (Equivalent Pattern on AWS)

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket         = "acme-prod-tfstate"
    key            = "network/terraform.tfstate"
    region         = "us-east-1"
    dynamodb_table = "terraform-locks"   # holds the LockID row while a plan/apply runs
    encrypt        = true
  }
}

resource "aws_dynamodb_table" "terraform_locks" {
  name         = "terraform-locks"
  billing_mode = "PAY_PER_REQUEST"
  hash_key     = "LockID"

  attribute {
    name = "LockID"
    type = "S"
  }
}
```

### What Happens Under the Hood

```text
  Engineer A: terraform apply         Engineer B: terraform apply
         │                                    │
         ▼                                    ▼
  ┌─────────────────┐                 ┌─────────────────┐
  │ Acquire lock     │  ──── OK ────►  │ (lock held by A) │
  │ (GCS generation/ │                 │ Acquire lock      │
  │  DynamoDB row)   │                 │ ──── BLOCKED ────►│  waits / errors
  └────────┬─────────┘                 └───────────────────┘
           ▼
  Read state → compute plan → apply → write new state → release lock
           │
           ▼
  Engineer B's apply now proceeds against the UPDATED state — no overwrite.
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: State locking prevents *concurrent corruption*, but it does not prevent *logical* drift (someone changing a resource by hand in the console). Pair remote state with `terraform plan` in CI on every PR (Section 3) to catch drift before it reaches `apply`.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.1: Enforcing Input Validation on Module Variables
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: A Typo That Became a $4,000 Bill

Someone consuming your `cloud-run-service` module passes `min_instances = 100` instead of `1` — a typo. Without validation, Terraform happily applies it: a Cloud Run service now keeps 100 warm instances running 24/7. Nobody notices until the monthly bill arrives.

Terraform's `validation` blocks catch this at `terraform plan` time — before anything is ever applied.

### Validated Module Inputs

```hcl
# modules/cloud-run-service/variables.tf
variable "min_instances" {
  type    = number
  default = 0

  validation {
    condition     = var.min_instances >= 0 && var.min_instances <= 5
    error_message = "min_instances must be between 0 and 5. For anything higher, get platform-team sign-off and hardcode it outside this module."
  }
}

variable "cpu_limit" {
  type    = string
  default = "1"

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["1", "2", "4", "8"], var.cpu_limit)
    error_message = "cpu_limit must be one of: 1, 2, 4, 8 (Cloud Run's supported vCPU tiers)."
  }
}

variable "environment" {
  type = string

  validation {
    condition     = contains(["dev", "staging", "prod"], var.environment)
    error_message = "environment must be exactly one of: dev, staging, prod."
  }
}
```

Running `terraform plan` with a bad value now fails fast, at design time, with a message that tells the caller exactly what to fix:

```text
$ terraform plan
╷
│ Error: Invalid value for variable
│
│   on environments/dev/main.tf line 12:
│   12: module "api" {
│
│ min_instances must be between 0 and 5. For anything higher, get
│ platform-team sign-off and hardcode it outside this module.
╵
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Validation blocks are documentation that Terraform enforces for you — write the `error_message` as if you were explaining the constraint to a teammate who has never read the module source.

lessons.title: Lesson 2.2: Isolating Environments — Workspaces vs. Directory-per-Environment
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: `terraform destroy` Run Against the Wrong Workspace

A teammate meant to tear down a stale `dev` sandbox. They ran `terraform workspace select dev` — except a typo in an earlier script had left the CLI on the `prod` workspace, and Terraform workspaces share the exact same `.tf` files and variable definitions. The `destroy` executed against production.

This is the core risk of **CLI workspaces**: because all environments share identical code and only differ by an in-state workspace name, a single wrong `workspace select` silently redirects a destructive command at the wrong environment.

### Comparison: Workspaces vs. Directory-per-Environment

| Approach | How it isolates | Blast radius of a mistake | Best for |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **CLI Workspaces** (`terraform workspace select`) | Same code, same backend config, different state file per workspace | High — a wrong `select` silently targets the wrong environment with identical tooling | Short-lived, symmetric environments (ephemeral PR-preview stacks) |
| **Directory-per-Environment** (this course's layout) | Separate `environments/<env>/` directories, each with its own `backend.tf` pointing at a different state bucket/prefix | Low — you must physically `cd` into `environments/prod/`, and typically use separate cloud credentials per environment | Production infrastructure with real compliance/blast-radius requirements |

### Directory-per-Environment in Practice

```hcl
# environments/prod/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "acme-prod-tfstate"   # different bucket entirely from dev
    prefix = "terraform/network"
  }
}

# environments/dev/backend.tf
terraform {
  backend "gcs" {
    bucket = "acme-dev-tfstate"    # physically separate state, separate GCP project
    prefix = "terraform/network"
  }
}
```

Because `prod` and `dev` point at entirely different buckets (and ideally different GCP projects/AWS accounts with separate credentials), there is no CLI flag that can accidentally point a `prod` apply at `dev` state, or vice versa — the isolation is structural, not a matter of remembering which workspace is selected.

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: Prefer directory-per-environment for anything with real production blast radius. Reserve CLI workspaces for cases where the *whole point* is spinning up and tearing down identical, disposable environments (like one stack per open pull request).

sections.title: Section 3: CI/CD Plan Checks & Automated Governance

lessons.title: Lesson 3.1: Automating `terraform plan` Checks in CI
lessons.body:
### The Scenario: The Plan Nobody Reviewed

A pull request changes a `variables.tf` default. It looks harmless in the diff. Nobody runs `terraform plan` locally before merging, and the next scheduled apply silently resizes a production database instance because the default flowed through to a `google_sql_database_instance` resource. The PR review only looked at code — it never saw what Terraform actually intended to *do*.

The fix: make `terraform plan` output part of the pull request itself, generated by CI, so reviewers see the real infrastructure diff — not just the HCL diff.

### GitHub Actions: Plan-on-PR, Apply-on-Merge

```yaml
# .github/workflows/terraform.yml
name: terraform
on:
  pull_request:
    paths: ["environments/**", "modules/**"]
  push:
    branches: [main]
    paths: ["environments/**", "modules/**"]

jobs:
  plan:
    if: github.event_name == 'pull_request'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3

      - name: Terraform Init
        working-directory: environments/prod
        run: terraform init -input=false

      - name: Terraform Plan
        id: plan
        working-directory: environments/prod
        run: terraform plan -input=false -no-color -out=tfplan | tee plan.txt

      - name: Comment Plan on PR
        uses: actions/github-script@v7
        with:
          script: |
            const fs = require('fs');
            const plan = fs.readFileSync('environments/prod/plan.txt', 'utf8').slice(0, 60000);
            github.rest.issues.createComment({
              issue_number: context.issue.number,
              owner: context.repo.owner,
              repo: context.repo.repo,
              body: `### Terraform Plan\n\`\`\`\n${plan}\n\`\`\``
            });

  apply:
    if: github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production   # requires a manual approval gate in GitHub Environments
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: hashicorp/setup-terraform@v3
      - working-directory: environments/prod
        run: terraform init -input=false
      - working-directory: environments/prod
        run: terraform apply -input=false -auto-approve
```

### Governance Pipeline

```text
 Pull Request opened
        │
        ▼
 ┌─────────────────┐     posts plan as PR comment
 │ terraform plan   │ ───────────────────────────► Human reviews REAL diff
 └────────┬─────────┘                                       │
          │                                                  ▼
          │                                        Approve & merge to main
          ▼                                                  │
 ┌─────────────────┐                                         ▼
 │ terraform fmt /  │                              ┌──────────────────┐
 │ validate / tflint│ ◄─── also runs on every PR ── │ terraform apply   │ (production
 └──────────────────┘                              │ (environment gate) environment)
```

💡 **Interactive Takeaway**: The manual `environment: production` approval gate in the `apply` job is what turns 'CI runs my Terraform' into 'CI *proposes*, a human *approves*'. Never wire `apply` to run unattended on every merge to `main` for anything with real blast radius — Atlantis and Spacelift offer the same plan-then-approve pattern as managed services if you outgrow raw GitHub Actions.

lessons.title: Lesson 3.2: Knowledge Check — Modules, State, and CI Governance
lessons.body:
**Question 1:** Two engineers run `terraform apply` against the same GCS-backed workspace within seconds of each other. What prevents state corruption?

A) Terraform automatically merges both plans
B) GCS backend locking blocks the second apply until the first releases its lock
C) Terraform refuses to run apply more than once per hour
D) Nothing — this always corrupts state

**Correct answer: B.** GCS (and S3+DynamoDB) backends acquire a lock before writing state; a concurrent `apply` blocks or errors instead of racing to overwrite the file.

---

**Question 2:** Why does directory-per-environment provide a smaller blast radius than CLI workspaces for production infrastructure?

A) It uses a different Terraform binary version
B) Each environment has physically separate backend configuration (state bucket/credentials), so there's no single `select` command that can misdirect a destructive operation
C) Workspaces are deprecated in modern Terraform
D) Directory-per-environment doesn't support modules

**Correct answer: B.** Workspaces share identical code and backend config, differing only by an in-state workspace name — a wrong `workspace select` silently retargets commands. Separate directories with separate `backend.tf` files make misdirection structurally impossible, not just a matter of discipline.

---

**Question 3:** What is the primary purpose of posting `terraform plan` output as a PR comment in CI?

A) To slow down the merge process
B) To let reviewers see the actual infrastructure diff Terraform intends to make, not just the HCL source diff
C) To replace `terraform apply` entirely
D) To satisfy a linter requirement

**Correct answer: B.** A code review of `.tf` file changes doesn't show what Terraform will *do* — a default value change can silently resize a production resource. Surfacing the real plan output turns review from 'does this HCL look right' into 'is this the change we actually want to make'.
